in associations in the field for which classification is sought, which require outstanding achievements of

C. Contributions
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(5) requires "[e]vidence of the alien's original
scientific, scholarly, or business-related contributions of major significance in the field." Analysis
under this criterion focuses on whether the beneficiary's original work constitutes major, significant
contributions in the field. 6
6 See generally 2 USC1S Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
4
Initially, the Petitioner submitted recommendation letters, praising the Beneficiary for his skills and
abilities and his work at various organizations. For instance, C-M-D-S- commented that the
Beneficiary "is a committed, honest, versatile, dynamic, and focused professional, with excellence in
relationships and teamwork, and proven delivery of results." However, the Petitioner did not
demonstrate how letters that show the Beneficiary's skills or abilities reflect original contributions of
major significance in the field. Cf, Skokos v. United States Dep 't of Homeland Sec., No.
209CV00193RLHPAL, 2010 WL 11538054, at *4 (D. Nev. Jan. 13, 2010), ajf'd sub nom. Skokos v.
US. Dep 't of Homeland Sec., 420 F. App'x 712 (9th Cir. 2011) (holding that while a skilled
professional in the field, there was no evidence to suggest the plaintiff's professional contributions are
original or that they have been of major significance); Soni v. United States, No. CV 11-2431, 2016
WL 4154137, at *5 (D.N.J. Aug. 2, 2016) (finding plaintiff's evidence described his work for employer
in general terms, such as vital, efficient, effective, outstanding, unique, extraordinary, critical, and
leading without detailing how his work has been of major significance in the field).
Furthermore, the Petitioner did not establish how the Beneficiary's work influenced or impacted the
overall field in a majorly significant manner rather than limited to the projects or organizations that
employed him. For example, M-F-G- indicated that the Beneficiary "carried out his activities in
technical support, on-site training of Yaskawa Robots and installed equipment, and with the technical
staff who would provide support to these pieces of equipment at the company." However, the
Petitioner did not show how the letters reflect that the Beneficiary's work at these places somehow
made a majorly significant contribution to the field as a whole. Cf, Aravamuthan v. Jaddou, No.
3:23-CV-01412-N, 2025 WL 1708126, at *6 (N.D. Tex. June 17, 2025) (upholding plaintiff did not
provide specific examples to show the major significance of his contributions in the field as a whole);
Bhanu v. Garland, No. CV 22-103, 2023 WL 6119357, at *8 (E.D. Pa. Sept. 18, 2023) (finding USCIS
did not introduce a novel evidentiary standard when it required that the petitioner show how his
contributions influenced the field as a whole); Visinscaia v. Beers, 4 F. Supp. 3d 126, 134 (D.D.C.
2013) (finding evidence must include "specific information relating to the impact" of the plaintiff's
work in the field as a whole).
In addition, the Petitioner submitted a letter from B-D-F- who indicated the Beneficiary's attendance
and participation at an "Open Housing Welding and Machining Event, where he presented our products
and delivered a training session in the field of Welding and Robotics." The Petitioner also submitted
a program for the welding seminar. However, the Petitioner did not contextualize or show the impact
of the Beneficiary's presentation. The Petitioner did not demonstrate, for example, that the
Beneficiary's presentation resulted in a majorly significant contribution in the field. Without
supporting documentation showing the impact, influence, or effect in the field in a majorly significant
manner, the Petitioner did not establish that simply presenting at a welding seminar indicates original
contributions of major significance in the field. Cf, Agrawal v. Miller, No. 4:24CV3143, 2025 WL
2879217, at *20 (D. Neb. Sept. 12, 2025) (upholding that attendance and presentation of material at
conferences is not uncommon in the scientific fields, nor is the publication of research in the field).
Detailed letters from experts in the field explaining the nature and significance of the beneficiary's
contribution may also provide valuable context for evaluating the claimed original contributions of
major significance, particularly when the record includes documentation corroborating the claimed
5
significance. 7 Submitted letters should specifically describe the beneficiary's contribution and its
significance in the field and should set forth the basis of the writer's knowledge and expertise. 8 Here,
the letters point to the Beneficiary's work but do not demonstrate how the field views it as original
contributions of major significance in the field, such as widespread impact or influence. Cf, Gadh ave
v. Thompson, No. 3:21-CV-2938-D, 2023 WL 6931334, at *5 (N.D. Tex. Oct. 19, 2023) (finding
testimonial letters contained mostly general, conclusory statements about the value of the petitioner's
research without explaining in detail specific ways in which his contributions have already been
widely applied or replicated to serve the industry); Jafarov v. United States Citizenship & Immigr.
Servs., No. 23 CIV. 3372 (PAE), 2024 WL 69056, at *8 (S.D.N.Y. Jan. 5, 2024) (finding the petitioner's
testimonial evidence spoke largely in generalities and did not evidence the tangible impact of his work
in the field); Noroozi v. Napolitano, 905 F. Supp. 2d 535, 544 (S.D.N.Y. 2012) (upholding reference
letters with limited detail on satisfaction of regulatory criterion insufficient to form the basis for
required evidence).
In the RFE response, the Petitioner contended:
USCIS has already accepted [the Beneficiary's] publications under the separate
"authorship of scholarly articles" criterion; the petitioner can now argue that the same
body of work also evidences "original scientific, scholarly, or business-related
contributions of major significance" because the articles document how [the
Beneficiary's] methodologies have been codified, analyzed, and taught as models for
industrial competitiveness and human-capital formation in automation engineering.
Although the Petitioner provided a self-compiled document listing a "Key Fact about [t he Beneficiary]
and "How It Shows Original Contribution of Major Significance," the document makes unsupported
assertions regarding the significance of the Beneficiary's "Key Fact." Moreover, evidence that the
beneficiary's work was funded, patented, or published, while potentially demonstrating the work's
originality, will not necessarily establish, on its own, that the work is of major significance in the
field. 9 Without evidence reflecting the impact, influence, or effect of the Beneficiary's authored
scholarly work, the Petitioner did not establish the Beneficiary's written work qualifies as
contributions of major significance. Documentation that published research has been highly cited
relative to other works in that field may be probative of the significance of the beneficiary's
°
contributions to the field of endeavor. 1 Cf, Kazarian v. US. Citizenship & Immigr. Servs., 580 F.3d
1030, 1036 (9th Cir. 2009), aff'd in part, 596 F.3d 1115 (9th Cir. 2010) (finding publications and
presentations alone are not sufficient to demonstrate major significance).
For the reasons discussed above, considered both individually and collectively, the Petitioner did not
demonstrate the Beneficiary meets this criterion.
